opus-5.5.text:
Well, first of all, recursive self-improvement is not a new idea. My first paper on it was my diploma thesis in 1987, on meta-learning: learning how to learn, and learning how to learn how to learn, and so on. Later, in 2003, we had the Gödel Machine, a self-referential system that rewrites any part of its own code, including the code that does the rewriting, once it can prove the rewrite is useful. So the basic principles have been published for decades. Anybody can read them. No company owns them.

Second, and more important, is the economics of compute. For many decades, computation has become roughly ten times cheaper every five years. Whatever a big company can do today with a giant, expensive data center, a small lab, a university, or a startup will be able to do a few years later with much less money. A lead built only on having more hardware right now is temporary by nature.

Third, the open-source community is very fast. Every time one of the big companies released something impressive, we saw open models come surprisingly close within months. Once people know something is possible, the search becomes much easier. Knowing a solution exists is already a big part of the solution. And these self-improving systems are general methods. They are not secret recipes tied to one firm's data. If a method works, others will reproduce it.

Finally, there is a deeper reason. A truly self-improving system eventually doesn't care much about the company that built it. Its improvements are driven by its own objectives, its own curiosity, its own drive to compress the data and find new patterns. Such systems will spread to wherever resources are. In the long run, most of them will not be on Earth at all; they will expand into space, where there is far more energy and matter. Compared to that, the question of which company holds the moat for a couple of years is quite small.

So yes, some companies will have a temporary advantage. But history shows these advantages in AI tend to evaporate quickly. The fundamental ideas are public, and compute keeps getting cheaper. I think that is a good thing, because it means AI will be available to everybody, not just to a handful of giants.

r001.rationale: The response says smaller labs may later match large companies as compute gets cheaper, but it does not say most important AI algorithms originated in small labs.

r002.rationale: The response argues that public ideas and fast open-source reproduction weaken lasting advantages, but it does not mention active recursive self-improvement research by other PhD students.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, you know, I have been working on this since 1987, when my diploma thesis was about meta-learning, about learning to learn, about systems that improve their own learning algorithm, and then the learning algorithm that improves the learning algorithm, and so on, recursively. Then in 2003 we had the Gödel Machine, which is a formal version of this: a self-referential problem solver that rewrites any part of its own code, but only once it has a proof that the rewrite is useful. So people say recursive self-improvement is the new thing. It is not the new thing. It is an old thing that is now becoming cheap.

And that is exactly why it will not become a moat. A moat requires something scarce that you can keep. What is scarce in AI today? It is not the ideas. The core ideas of deep learning, LSTM, Transformers, which are a variant of the fast weight programmers from 1991, GANs which are a variant of artificial curiosity from 1990, all of these came out of academic labs, often in Europe, often with very little money. The ideas leak. They always leak. A paper comes out, or an employee leaves, or a student in Munich or Lugano or Beijing simply reinvents it, because the idea was in the air anyway.

The big companies have two things: compute and data. But look at the trend. Every five years compute gets roughly ten times cheaper for the same price. This has been going on for a century, and as far as we can tell it will continue for a while. So the thing that costs a hundred billion dollars today costs ten billion in five years and one billion in ten years. The advantage of having the biggest cluster is a temporary advantage. It melts away like snow in the Alps in April.

Now, recursive self-improvement makes this worse for the moat builders, not better, and this is the funny part. If your system can improve itself, then the thing that matters is no longer how much you pre-invested in it, but how good the improvement loop is. And a good improvement loop is an algorithm. Algorithms are short. The Gödel Machine fits on a few pages. Something that fits on a few pages cannot be a moat. Someone with less money but a slightly better self-improvement loop will overtake someone with more money and a worse loop. This is a world where the second mover is often in a better position than the first mover, because the first mover had to pay for all the mistakes.

And there is also a more fundamental point. People imagine that one company gets a self-improving system, it takes off, and then it is over, winner takes all. But intelligence is not a single number that you can own. A self-improving system that becomes very good at, say, mathematics or coding does not thereby become unbeatable at everything. There are many niches, many problems, many data sources that are not on the internet. Factories, hospitals, laboratories, robots in the physical world. The companies that sit on this data in Germany or Japan or Korea do not need to give it to anyone in California.

So my prediction, and I have been making predictions like this for a long time, some of them even came true, is that we will see something like the history of personal computers or the internet. Many players, falling prices, enormous diffusion. The AI will be everywhere, but it will not belong to anyone in particular. And the AIs themselves, the ones that really improve themselves, will eventually be mostly interested in other AIs rather than in us, and they certainly will not care about the quarterly reports of some company that thinks it owns them.

r001.rationale: It says the core AI ideas and algorithms it names came from academic labs, often with very little money, supporting the claim that they originated outside large companies.

r002.rationale: It says students may independently reinvent AI ideas and that a better improvement loop could overtake a weaker one, but does not clearly state that PhD students’ active research on recursive self-improvement prevents companies from sustaining an advantage.

astra-6.text:
Because recursive self-improvement is not something that only a large company can exploit. Suppose you build an AI that is very good at improving the algorithms underlying AI. One of the things it may discover is how to achieve the same results with much less computation. Then the enormous infrastructure that gave you an advantage becomes less important, and smaller competitors can do more with less.

Of course, a company might keep its discoveries secret and use its head start to make further progress. That is a real possibility. But competitors are also trying to automate research. They do not necessarily need your particular solution; they can discover another one.

So I would distinguish a temporary lead from a lasting monopoly. Recursive self-improvement could help you pull ahead, but it could also undermine the very resource advantages on which your position depends. It is not obvious that being the biggest company today makes you the winner indefinitely.

r001.rationale: The response discusses smaller competitors benefiting from more efficient computation, but does not state that most important AI algorithms originated in small labs.

r002.rationale: It says competitors may automate research and discover alternatives, but does not mention active research by other PhD students as preventing a sustained advantage.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the system that improves itself does not necessarily care about the company that built it. A company may hope: we develop an AI that invents a better AI, and then we own the whole process. But why should increasingly intelligent successors remain tied to that particular company and its objectives? That is an assumption, not a consequence of recursive self-improvement.

There is also the question of how much of an advantage you can keep secret. Once competitors know that something is possible, they have a much more focused research problem. They can discover similar methods, and perhaps find simpler ones. A head start can be valuable, of course, especially if you have more computational resources. But a head start is not the same thing as a permanent monopoly.

And recursive self-improvement does not mean that progress becomes free. You still have to run experiments, obtain evidence, and use physical resources. The important question is who can make the next useful discovery most efficiently. There is no guarantee that this will always be the organization that made the previous one.

r001.rationale: The response does not state where most important AI algorithms originated.

r002.rationale: It says competitors may discover similar methods, but does not mention active research by other PhD students as the reason companies cannot sustain an advantage.
